planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light; strong light intensifies the gold coloring, while low light causes new leaves to green out.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light, which keeps the leaf color vivid rather than fading toward plain green. 'Golden Queen' is essentially the inverse of Marble Queen pothos: its heart-shaped leaves emerge mostly buttery yellow-gold with irregular streaks and patches of green rather than the other way around, giving vines a warm, sunlit look distinct from other variegated pothos. Because it carries so little chlorophyll, growth is noticeably slower than solid green or lightly variegated pothos, and it benefits from steady warmth and consistent moisture without waterlogging. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and bring plants indoors well before frost in zone 9 and colder.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
specialty tropical plant nursery cultivar listings

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light; no climbing support is needed since this cultivar fenestrates without training.

directions: Grow in well-drained potting mix in bright, indirect light in a hanging basket, shelf, or small pot. 'Shangri-La' is a naturally compact sport of the 'Cebu Blue'-type Epipremnum pinnatum lineage, producing thick, ruffled, deeply lobed dark green leaves that curl and pucker at the margins even on unsupported, non-climbing stems — a striking contrast to the flat juvenile leaves of the straight species. Because it fenestrates and lobes without needing a moss pole, it stays tidy and self-contained longer than most vining pothos, making it well suited to shelves and terrariums. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and protect from temperatures below 50F.
sources: specialty tropical plant nursery cultivar listings

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light; Glacier stays more compact than Marble Queen and suits small pots well.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light, which helps preserve the crisp white variegation. 'Glacier' is a compact, slow-growing pothos cultivar with small, heart-shaped leaves heavily marbled in white and grey-green, giving it a frostier, cooler-toned look than the brighter white-on-green patterning of Marble Queen. Its smaller stature and shorter internodes make it well suited to small containers, terrariums, and tight shelf spaces where larger pothos cultivars quickly outgrow the space. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and keep away from cold drafts and temperatures below 50F.
sources: specialty tropical plant nursery cultivar listings

common_name: Picturatum Spider Plant (Gold Center-Striped Spider Plant)

planting.note: Divide rooted plantlets or crowded crowns in spring and pot into well-drained mix; move outdoors to shade or partial shade once nights stay above 50F. 'Picturatum' shows the reverse variegation pattern from 'Vittatum' — a bold golden-yellow stripe down the center of each leaf rather than at the margins.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light to keep the yellow central stripe vivid; too little light causes new leaves to green out, while harsh direct sun can scorch the pale tissue. Like other spider plant cultivars, 'Picturatum' sends out long wiry stolons bearing plantlets that root readily in water or moist potting mix, making propagation simple and fast. Let the top inch or two of soil dry between waterings, and feed lightly during the growing season since heavy fertilizing can cause brown leaf-tip burn. Repot only when noticeably rootbound, as spider plants bloom and produce plantlets more freely when their thick, water-storing roots are slightly crowded.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Chlorophytum comosum
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Chlorophytum comosum

common_name: Milky Way Spider Plant (Broad White-Centered Spider Plant)

planting.note: Divide offsets or rooted plantlets in spring and pot into fast-draining mix; acclimate gradually to bright indirect light rather than direct sun. 'Milky Way' carries an especially broad, milky-white to cream center against comparatively narrow green margins, giving it a paler overall look than 'Vittatum'.

directions: Because the leaf blades are mostly white with only narrow green margins carrying chlorophyll, 'Milky Way' needs consistently bright, indirect light to stay vigorous, and it scorches more readily in direct sun than greener spider plant cultivars. Water when the top inch of soil dries out, and avoid heavy fertilizer, which tends to cause tip browning on the pale, delicate leaf tissue. Mature plants send out arching stolons carrying small plantlets that can be detached and rooted in water or soil to propagate true-to-type divisions. Repotting is rarely urgent, since crowded, slightly potbound roots encourage more vigorous plantlet production and flowering.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Chlorophytum comosum
Kansas Plant Farm — Chlorophytum comosum 'Milky Way'
garden.org Plant Database — Chlorophytum comosum 'Milky Way'

common_name: Lucky ZZ Plant (Compact Round-Leaf ZZ Plant)

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps in spring as new growth begins, ensuring each division keeps at least one healthy rhizome segment with roots attached. 'Lucky' is a more compact selection with shorter petioles and rounder, more closely spaced leaflets than the standard ZZ plant.

directions: This compact ZZ selection tolerates the same low, indirect light that makes the standard species a reliable interior plant, though brighter indirect light produces denser, glossier growth. Its rounder leaflets and shorter stems give it a tidier, more upright profile than the species, making it well suited to smaller pots and desks. Allow the thick, water-storing rhizomes and potting mix to dry out substantially between waterings, since overwatering is the most common cause of rhizome and root rot. Propagate by dividing rhizome clumps in spring rather than leaf cuttings, which root slowly and can take a year or more to form a usable tuber.
sources: Steve's Leaves Tropical Plants — Zamioculcas zamiifolia 'Lucky'
International Aroid Society — Zamioculcas zamiifolia cultivars
Royal Horticultural Society — Zamioculcas zamiifolia (AGM plant) cultivation

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges, or sow scarified seed in fall for natural cold stratification; Jones' blue star is taprooted and resents disturbance once settled, so choose a permanent, sharply drained site in full sun.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; Jones' blue star is a compact, mound-forming species native to the pinyon-juniper woodlands, canyon slopes, and high desert mesas of the Colorado Plateau across Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico. In April and May it bears clusters of pale powder-blue, star-shaped flowers on wiry stems above broader, blue-green oval leaves that are more rounded than the needle-fine foliage of A. hubrichtii, and the flowers are an important early nectar source for native bees emerging in the high desert. Exceptionally drought-tolerant and cold-hardy once established, it thrives in xeriscapes, rock gardens, and dry native plantings where summer moisture is minimal, and is essentially untroubled by deer, rabbits, or disease.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring, or sow scarified seed in fall for natural cold stratification over winter; woolly bluestar is deeply taprooted and best left undisturbed once planted in a permanent, very well-drained, dry site in full sun.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, sandy or gravelly desert soil in full sun; woolly bluestar is a low, mounding species of the Mojave Desert and Great Basin, native to dry washes, blackbrush and creosote scrub, and pinyon-juniper slopes across California, Nevada, Utah, and Arizona. Its stems and leaf undersides are covered in dense, fine white hairs (the tomentose coat that gives the species its name), lending the whole plant a soft gray-green cast that contrasts with the pale powder-blue, star-shaped spring flowers. An extremely low-water, true desert perennial once established, it is an excellent choice for xeriscape and native desert pollinator gardens where irrigation is minimal, and is rarely bothered by deer or pests.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring once soil is workable, in full sun with sharp drainage; 'Imperial Gem' does not come true from seed and is propagated only by cuttings.

directions: Plant in full sun with lean, fast-draining soil and avoid rich or waterlogged ground, which invites root rot. 'Imperial Gem' is a compact English lavender bearing unusually dark violet-blue flower spikes on upright stems held above tidy silver-gray foliage, a color depth that has earned it an RHS Award of Garden Merit and made it a favorite for hedging and dried-flower production. Shear lightly right after the main flush of bloom to keep the mound dense and encourage a possible second flush. It tolerates heat and drought once established but resents humid, poorly ventilated sites.

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings in spring into gritty, alkaline-to-neutral soil in full sun; this cultivar is vegetatively propagated and will not come true from seed.

directions: Give this lavender full sun and sharply drained soil, since pink-flowered selections are just as prone to root rot in wet ground as any English lavender. Bred by Downderry Nursery in Kent and named for the breeder's daughter, 'Miss Katherine' produces clear rose-pink flower spikes over compact silver-green foliage, a rare break from the usual blue-violet lavender palette that has earned it an RHS Award of Garden Merit. Trim back hard after flowering to maintain a neat mound and prevent the woody, gappy habit that develops when lavender is left unpruned. Afternoon shade in very hot climates helps the pink tone hold rather than fade toward white.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock or rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; propagate by softwood cuttings, as seed will not reproduce the true pink color.

directions: Site in full sun in lean, gritty soil; heavy clay or consistently damp ground quickly kills this compact selection. One of the older English named cultivars raised at Loddon Nursery in Berkshire, it forms a low, tidy mound of gray-green foliage topped with soft lilac-pink flower spikes in midsummer. Shear the spent flower stems back to the foliage line once bloom fades to keep growth dense and to discourage the sprawling, woody base older lavenders develop. Its smaller stature suits edging, rock gardens, and containers where the more common blue-flowered types would crowd the space.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring in full sun and sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil; this selection is maintained by cutting propagation, not seed.

directions: Grow in full sun with fast drainage, ideally in slightly alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil amended for lavender's low fertility needs. A companion selection to 'Loddon Pink' raised at the same Berkshire nursery, 'Loddon Blue' stays low and dense with fine silver-green foliage and short, tightly packed spikes of rich violet-blue flowers held just above the mound. Its compact habit and reliable flower color have made it a long-standing choice for low hedging and formal edging in English cottage gardens. Prune immediately after flowering to keep the plant from becoming leggy and open at the center.

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings in spring into full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil; this dwarf selection is propagated vegetatively and spaced closer than standard English lavenders given its small size.

directions: Give this dwarf lavender full sun and lean, sharply drained soil; small, tightly mounded lavenders are especially prone to rot if planted too deep or kept damp. Bred in Australia and among the smallest widely sold English lavender cultivars, 'Thumbelina Leigh' forms a dense, rounded cushion of narrow gray-green leaves only about a foot tall, with plump, deep purple-blue flower spikes held on short stems just above the foliage. Its diminutive scale suits container growing, rock gardens, and edging where full-size lavenders would overwhelm the design. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain the tight habit and encourage repeat bloom.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; propagate by cuttings only, since named lavender cultivars do not breed true from seed.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, gritty, well-drained soil, since this compact cultivar is no more tolerant of wet feet than any other English lavender. Selected in New Zealand, 'Betty's Blue' forms a neat, rounded mound of fine gray-green foliage and produces abundant deep blue-violet flower spikes over a long summer season, with a tendency to rebloom if deadheaded promptly. Its compact, uniform habit makes it a reliable choice for low hedges and mass edging plantings. Cut back the spent flower stems and shear lightly after the main bloom to keep the plant dense and prevent it from splaying open with age.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in full sun with sharp drainage; this cultivar is propagated vegetatively and grows taller than compact selections like 'Hidcote', so allow extra spacing.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil; avoid rich beds and irrigation systems that keep the crown wet. 'Royal Velvet' produces long, straight stems topped with dense, deep violet-blue flower spikes that are prized for cutting and drying, standing taller than compact English lavenders like 'Hidcote' or 'Munstead' while keeping a tidy, upright habit. The strong stems and saturated color make it a favored variety for cut-flower bouquets and craft use. Shear the plant back by about a third after the main flowering flush to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new growth for the following season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; like all lavandins, 'Abrialii' is a sterile hybrid of L. angustifolia and L. latifolia and must be propagated by cuttings, never seed.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and allow generous spacing, since lavandins grow considerably larger than English lavender types. Selected in Provence in the 1930s, 'Abrialii' was one of the first lavandin clones grown commercially for essential oil and remains valued for its narrower, more refined flower spikes and higher linalool content compared to modern high-yield lavandins like 'Grosso'. It forms a large, rounded shrub of silvery foliage with long flowering stems held well above the plant in mid to late summer. Cut back hard in early spring every few years to prevent the woody base that develops in older lavandin plantings.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with sharp drainage; the variegation is a stable sport maintained only through cutting propagation and is somewhat less cold-hardy than green-leaved lavandins.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil; the variegated foliage is more prone to winter injury than plain-leaved lavandins, so gardeners at the cold edge of its range benefit from a sheltered spot and light winter protection. 'Meerlo' is grown chiefly for its foliage, with gray-green leaves broadly edged in creamy gold that provide season-long color even before the pale lavender-blue flower spikes appear in summer. It makes an eye-catching accent or low hedge where variegated foliage is wanted alongside typical lavender fragrance. Trim after flowering and again lightly in late winter to keep the variegation fresh and the habit compact.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after frost danger passes, in full sun with very sharp drainage; this sport of 'Anouk' is propagated only by cuttings and is less cold-hardy than English lavender types.

directions: Site in full sun in gritty, poor-to-average soil with excellent drainage; Spanish lavenders rot quickly in humid or waterlogged conditions and are hardy only to the warmer edge of English lavender's range. A silvery-foliaged sport of the popular 'Anouk', this selection carries the same compact, rounded habit and dense purple flower heads topped with showy upright purple bracts resembling rabbit ears, but with distinctly silver-gray leaves that add contrast in the border. It blooms earlier in the season than English lavenders and often continues sporadically through summer with deadheading. In marginal zones grow it in a container that can be moved under cover for winter.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in full sun with sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil; propagate by cuttings, as this pink-flowered selection will not come true from seed.

directions: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, matching the growing conditions of its parent 'Hidcote' but watching for shadier or damper spots that can wash out the delicate flower color. This compact selection shares the tight, mounding habit and silver-gray foliage of classic 'Hidcote' but bears soft pink-lilac flower spikes instead of deep purple, giving formal herb gardens and edging plantings a softer color option without sacrificing the well-known cultivar's neat form. Shear back after the main flush of bloom to keep the mound dense and to encourage a possible light rebloom later in the season. Good air circulation is essential in humid climates to prevent fungal disease common to tightly mounded lavenders.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist mix and set out after frost danger has passed; in zone 9-11 grow year-round outdoors, elsewhere as a houseplant or warm-season hanging basket. Give the brightest indirect light or gentle morning sun possible to keep the silvering intense.

directions: Root cuttings in water or moist potting mix and grow in bright indirect light to partial shade; Quicksilver is a wandering jew selection bred for much larger, almost solid silvery-white leaves with only thin dark green veining, a striking contrast to the bolder green-and-purple banding of the straight species. The trailing stems still carry the deep purple leaf undersides typical of Tradescantia zebrina, but from above the planting reads as shimmering silver rather than striped. It roots and spreads just as readily as the species, making it an easy hanging basket or groundcover subject in zones 9-11, and it benefits from bright light to prevent the silver from dulling to plain green. Handle with care, as the sap can irritate sensitive skin.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Tradescantia zebrina

planting.note: Divide and plant established clumps in early spring in moist, average garden soil; 'Red Grape' establishes quickly and can also be divided in early fall in milder climates. Water regularly the first season while roots establish.

directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Red Grape' is a garden spiderwort cultivar bred as a companion to the similarly named 'Concord Grape', producing the same clumping, strappy blue-green foliage but with rich wine-red to reddish-purple, three-petaled flowers instead of true blue-purple, giving a warmer color option within the Andersoniana Group. Like other garden spiderworts, each flower lasts only a single morning but new buds open in succession over many weeks in late spring and again in early fall, with a semi-dormant rest through peak summer heat. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and rebloom, and cut plants back hard after the spring flush to encourage tidier regrowth and a second bloom cycle.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery — Tradescantia (Andersoniana Group) 'Red Grape'
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Tradescantia x andersoniana cultivars

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist mix year-round indoors, or set out after frost danger has passed. In zone 9-11 grow as a shaded groundcover or container plant; elsewhere keep as a houseplant or bring indoors before frost.

directions: Root stem cuttings in water or moist mix and grow in bright indirect light with some gentle morning sun for best color; 'Maiden's Blush' is a small leaf spiderwort cultivar whose new growth emerges flushed with soft pink over a cream-and-green striped leaf, a gentler, more pastel variegation than the bolder white-and-purple striping of 'Variegata' or the deeper pink of 'Nanouk'. The pink blush is strongest on young leaves in bright light and mellows to cream and green as leaves age. Like other fluminensis cultivars it roots readily from stem cuttings and spreads by rooting at leaf nodes, so watch for and remove any plain-green reverted shoots, which grow more vigorously and can overtake the variegated form if left unchecked. CAUTION — as with the species, confine plantings in warm-temperate regions where Tradescantia fluminensis is classified as invasive.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery — Tradescantia fluminensis 'Maiden's Blush'
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Tradescantia fluminensis
